tool.name: logging
tool.tagline: The standard library's flexible logging framework for apps and libraries
tool.description: logging is Python's built-in system for recording what a program does, with levels, named loggers, pluggable handlers and formatters. Every serious application and library uses it, and frameworks such as Django, FastAPI and Celery plug into it. Learning it well means readable diagnostics in development and searchable, structured logs in production.

glossary.def: In Python's logging: an object you send log messages to, named after a part of your program (like myapp.db). It decides which messages to pass on.
The logger at the top of the tree. Every other logger passes its messages up to it, and logging.info() and friends use it directly.
How important a log message is: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR or CRITICAL. A setting can hide every message below a chosen level.
In Python's logging: an object that sends log messages to one destination, such as the screen, a file or a network service.
In Python's logging: an object that lays out each log message as a line of text, for example putting the time and level in front.
The object Python's logging creates for each message, holding its text and values, level, time, logger name, line number and more.
In Python's logging: a logger handing each message it accepts up to its parent loggers' handlers as well as its own.
A Python variable (contextvars.ContextVar) whose value is kept separately for each thread and each asyncio task, so work running at the same time doesn't mix values up.
Writing each log entry as data with named fields, usually one JSON object per line, instead of a free-text sentence, so tools can search and filter by field.

concepts.name: Your first log messages
concepts.summary: Swap print() for real log messages using logging.basicConfig and the five standard level functions.
concepts.why: Log messages can be filtered, sent to a file and stamped with the time without touching the code that writes them; print() can't do that.
concepts.body:
**Logging** means having your program write short notes about what it's doing, like a ship's logbook, so you can see later what happened, especially when something went wrong. Each note is a log message.

Python's `logging` module gives each message a **level** saying how important it is: `DEBUG` (details for when you **debug**, that is, hunt down a bug), `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR` and `CRITICAL`, from least to most serious.

The quickest start is `logging.basicConfig(...)`, called once when your program starts. It sets the lowest level to show and the layout of each line. Messages go to **standard error** (stderr): a second output channel, next to normal output, that also shows in the terminal.

```python
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
```

Messages below the chosen level are dropped. With no setup at all, only `WARNING` and above appear: that's why `logging.info("hi")` seems to do nothing at first. The functions `logging.info`, `logging.warning`... call `basicConfig()` for you if nothing has been set up yet.

Why bother instead of `print`?

- You can turn detail up or down with one setting instead of deleting prints.
- Output goes to the terminal, a file or a log service without code changes.
- Each line can carry a **timestamp** (the date and time it was written), level, module and line number for free.

`basicConfig` does nothing if logging was already set up. That surprises people in Jupyter notebooks, in test tools, and after an early `logging.warning(...)` call (which sets it up for you). Pass `force=True` to replace the existing setup. Other handy arguments: `filename=` to write to a file and `datefmt=` for the timestamp layout.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys

logging.warning("before config")   # WARNING:root:before config (auto basicConfig)
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(levelname)-8s %(message)s",
    stream=sys.stdout,
    force=True,                     # replace any earlier configuration
)
logging.debug("hidden: below INFO")
logging.info("server started on port %d", 8000)
logging.error("disk almost full")
# INFO     server started on port 8000
# ERROR    disk almost full
takeaways: Five levels: DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL
Call logging.basicConfig once at startup to set the level and line layout
With no setup, logging shows only WARNING and above
pitfalls: Calling basicConfig after something else set up logging; it silently does nothing unless force=True.

quiz.q: With no logging configuration, what does logging.info('x') print?
quiz.explain: The default threshold is WARNING, so INFO messages are dropped.

concepts.name: Named loggers: getLogger(__name__)
concepts.summary: Create one logger per module with logging.getLogger(__name__) instead of sending everything to the root logger.
concepts.why: Named loggers tell you where each message came from and let you tune modules independently.
concepts.body:
Calling `logging.info(...)` sends the message to the **root logger**, the main logger at the top. Real code creates a **logger** (an object you send messages to) for each module, named after it:

```python
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
```

`getLogger` returns the same object for the same name every time, so creating it at the top of a module is cheap and safe. `__name__` is the module's own name, like `myapp.db.models` for the file `myapp/db/models.py`, so logger names follow your package's folders. That matters because:

- `%(name)s` in the line layout shows which module wrote each line,
- you can raise or lower the level of one part of your program: `logging.getLogger("myapp.db").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)`,
- third-party libraries do the same, so you can quiet them: `logging.getLogger("urllib3").setLevel(logging.WARNING)`.

Logger methods match the module's functions: `log.debug`, `log.info`, `log.warning`, `log.error`, `log.critical`, `log.exception`, plus `log.log(level, msg)`.

Don't create loggers with names that change for each user or each object: loggers are never deleted, so they pile up and use more and more memory. And never create `logging.Logger(...)` directly; always go through `getLogger`, so the new logger is linked into the tree of loggers.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, stream=sys.stdout,
                    format="%(name)s | %(levelname)s | %(message)s")

db_log = logging.getLogger("myapp.db")
api_log = logging.getLogger("myapp.api")
print(db_log is logging.getLogger("myapp.db"))   # True: same object

db_log.info("connected")
api_log.info("listening")
logging.getLogger("myapp.db").setLevel(logging.WARNING)  # quiet the db
db_log.info("query took 3 ms")                    # suppressed
api_log.info("GET /users")
# myapp.db | INFO | connected
# myapp.api | INFO | listening
# myapp.api | INFO | GET /users
takeaways: log = logging.getLogger(__name__) at the top of each module
Same name, same logger object
Names form a dotted tree you can tune part by part
pitfalls: Logging through the root logger everywhere, losing the module name and per-module control.

quiz.q: What do two calls to logging.getLogger('app.db') return?
options: A logger and a child logger
quiz.explain: logging keeps one logger per name and hands back the same one every time.

concepts.name: Choosing and filtering levels
concepts.summary: Pick the right level for each message and understand how logger levels filter them.
concepts.why: Using levels consistently is what makes logs easy to search, and lets tools alert you only about real problems.
concepts.body:
Each level has a number: `DEBUG` 10, `INFO` 20, `WARNING` 30, `ERROR` 40, `CRITICAL` 50. A logger passes a message on only if the message's level is at or above the logger's **effective level**, the threshold actually in force.

A practical guide:

- `DEBUG`: details that help when hunting a bug, such as the data received and which branch of an `if` ran. Switched off on the live system that real users use.
- `INFO`: normal milestones, such as startup, a job finishing, a user signing in.
- `WARNING`: something unexpected that was handled, such as trying an operation a second time, or an option that's being phased out.
- `ERROR`: an operation failed; someone should look.
- `CRITICAL`: the program may not be able to continue.

`logger.setLevel(level)` sets a threshold. A logger left at `NOTSET` (0) takes the level of its nearest parent logger that has one (`myapp` is the parent of `myapp.db`), ending at the root (`WARNING` by default). `logger.getEffectiveLevel()` tells you the result.

Levels accept names as strings: `setLevel("DEBUG")` works. That's handy when the level comes from an **environment variable**: a named setting you give a program from outside when you start it, like `LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`. `logging.getLevelNamesMapping()` (3.11+) gives the name-to-number dict.

When building a message is expensive (turning a huge object into text), guard it with `if log.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG):` so the work is skipped when DEBUG messages are switched off.
concepts.code:
import logging, os, sys
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

log = logging.getLogger("worker")
print(log.level, log.getEffectiveLevel())    # 0 30  (NOTSET, inherits WARNING)

log.setLevel(os.environ.get("LOG_LEVEL", "INFO"))
print(logging.getLevelName(log.getEffectiveLevel()))  # INFO
log.debug("payload=%s", {"id": 1})           # dropped
log.info("job started")                      # INFO job started
if log.isEnabledFor(logging.DEBUG):
    log.debug("expensive dump: %s", "...")   # skipped entirely
print(logging.getLevelNamesMapping()["ERROR"])  # 40
takeaways: DEBUG 10, INFO 20, WARNING 30, ERROR 40, CRITICAL 50
A NOTSET logger takes its level from its nearest parent
isEnabledFor() skips expensive message preparation
pitfalls: Logging normal events at ERROR, which floods alerts and hides real failures.

quiz.q: A logger 'app.db' is NOTSET; 'app' is set to DEBUG; root is WARNING. What is app.db's effective level?
quiz.explain: A NOTSET logger goes up to the nearest parent with a level set, here 'app'.

concepts.name: Message arguments and formats
concepts.summary: Pass values as separate arguments so text is only built when needed, and set each line's layout with format fields.
concepts.why: Separate arguments save work and let tools group similar messages; format fields add useful details for free.
concepts.body:
Logging methods take a message pattern and the values to put in it: `log.info("user %s logged in from %s", user, ip)`. Each `%s` is a placeholder. The values are merged in **only if the message is actually shown**, so a dropped DEBUG call costs almost nothing. With an f-string, the text is built every time, even when the message is thrown away.

Arguments also keep the pattern the same every time ("user %s logged in"). Log collection services such as Sentry use that to group identical events. Use `%s` (any value as text), `%d` (whole number), `%r` (Python's repr), `%.2f` (number with 2 decimals). The message pattern always uses this %-style.

The layout of each line is set by a format string made of **fields** (named pieces of information) of the **LogRecord**, the object logging creates for each message:

- `%(asctime)s`, `%(levelname)s`, `%(name)s`, `%(message)s`,
- `%(module)s`, `%(funcName)s`, `%(lineno)d`, `%(process)d`, `%(threadName)s`.

You can write the format string in `{}`-style instead by passing `style="{"` to `basicConfig`: `"{asctime} {levelname:<8} {message}"`. `datefmt` sets the layout of `asctime` with the `%` date codes of `strftime`, like `%Y-%m-%d`.

If a message has placeholders but the arguments don't match, logging doesn't crash your program: it prints a "--- Logging error ---" report with a traceback to stderr and carries on.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(
    stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.DEBUG, style="{",
    format="{levelname:<7} {funcName}:{lineno} {message}",
)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def handle(user, ms):
    log.info("user %s served in %.1f ms", user, ms)
    log.setLevel(logging.INFO)
    log.debug("details for %s", user)   # dropped: the text is never built

handle("ada", 12.345)
# INFO    handle:9 user ada served in 12.3 ms
takeaways: Pass values as arguments: log.info('x=%s', x), not f-strings
Values are merged into the text only when the message is actually shown
Format strings use LogRecord fields like %(name)s and %(lineno)d
pitfalls: Using f-strings in DEBUG calls inside code that runs very often, paying to build the text even when DEBUG is off.

quiz.q: Why prefer log.debug('data=%s', data) over log.debug(f'data={data}')?
options: f-strings are not allowed in logging
The %-version is only merged into text if the message is actually shown
The f-string version logs at INFO
The %-version also prints the variable's name
quiz.explain: The arguments are merged into the message later, only after the level check lets it through.

concepts.name: Handlers and formatters
concepts.summary: Send log messages to several places at once, each with its own level and layout, using handlers and formatters.
concepts.why: Real apps log to the console and files or services at once, with different detail for each.
concepts.body:
A logger decides **whether** a message is logged; **handlers** decide **where** it goes, and **formatters** decide **how** it looks as text. One logger can have many handlers.

Common handlers:

- `StreamHandler(sys.stderr)`: the console.
- `FileHandler("app.log")`: a file.
- `RotatingFileHandler(path, maxBytes=..., backupCount=...)` and `TimedRotatingFileHandler(path, when="midnight")` in `logging.handlers`: files that are rotated. When the file gets too big, or a day ends, it is renamed and a fresh one started, keeping only the last few.
- `SysLogHandler`, `SMTPHandler` (email), `HTTPHandler` (a web service), `QueueHandler`: other destinations.

Each handler has its own level, so the logger can let DEBUG through while the console handler shows only INFO and a file handler keeps everything. A message must pass the logger's level, then each handler's level, separately.

Wire it up by hand:

```python
h = logging.FileHandler("app.log", encoding="utf-8")
h.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)
h.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s %(name)s %(message)s"))
logger.addHandler(h)
```

`basicConfig` is just a shortcut that does this for the root logger. Attach handlers in one place at startup, usually to the root logger, not in every module, or you'll get duplicate lines.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys

log = logging.getLogger("app")
log.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)                 # logger lets everything through

console = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
console.setLevel(logging.INFO)
console.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("console: %(levelname)s %(message)s"))

file = logging.FileHandler("app.log", mode="w", encoding="utf-8")
file.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(levelname)s:%(name)s:%(message)s"))

log.addHandler(console)
log.addHandler(file)
log.debug("cache miss for key=42")
log.info("request done")
print(open("app.log").read())
# console: INFO request done
# DEBUG:app:cache miss for key=42
# INFO:app:request done
takeaways: Loggers filter, handlers send, formatters lay out the text
Each handler has its own level and formatter
Rotating handlers in logging.handlers keep log files from growing forever
pitfalls: Calling addHandler inside a function that runs many times, multiplying every log line.

quiz.q: The logger is at DEBUG, a console handler at WARNING. Where does log.info('x') appear?
options: Nowhere via that handler: it fails the handler's level
Only if the root is at INFO
quiz.explain: The record passes the logger but the handler drops anything below WARNING.

concepts.name: Propagation and the logger tree
concepts.summary: Follow how messages travel up the dotted tree of loggers to their parents' handlers, and fix duplicate log lines.
concepts.why: Propagation explains most 'why is this logged twice' and 'why is this not logged' puzzles.
concepts.body:
Loggers form a tree by name: `app.db.pool` is a child of `app.db`, which is a child of `app`, which is a child of the root logger. When a logger accepts a message, the message goes to that logger's own handlers and then, because `propagate` is True by default, to the handlers of each parent in turn, up to the root. This passing up is called **propagation**.

Two details trip people up:

- Parent **logger levels are not checked** on the way up; only the first logger's effective level and each **handler's** level are. A DEBUG message from `app.db` reaches the root's handlers even if the root logger is set to WARNING.
- If both `app` and the root have handlers, a message from `app.x` is printed by both: duplicate lines.

The standard design avoids both: put handlers only on the root logger (or one top-level application logger), leave module loggers without handlers, and control how much is shown with levels. Set `logger.propagate = False` only when one branch must go somewhere else exclusively, such as a separate security record of who did what.

If no handler is found anywhere, logging falls back to `logging.lastResort`, which prints WARNING and above to stderr. That's the bare message you see before setting anything up.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys

def show(msg):
    h = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
    h.setFormatter(logging.Formatter(msg + " %(name)s: %(message)s"))
    return h

root = logging.getLogger()
root.addHandler(show("[root]"))
root.setLevel(logging.WARNING)

app = logging.getLogger("app")
app.setLevel(logging.INFO)
app.addHandler(show("[app]"))

logging.getLogger("app.db").info("connected")   # handled twice
# [app] app.db: connected
# [root] app.db: connected   (root's WARNING level isn't checked)

app.propagate = False
logging.getLogger("app.db").info("pooled")
# [app] app.db: pooled
takeaways: Messages go to their logger's handlers, then every parent's handlers
Parent logger levels are skipped; only handler levels apply on the way up
Set up handlers once, on the root, to avoid duplicates
pitfalls: Adding a handler to a module logger and to the root, then seeing every line twice.

quiz.q: Root logger is WARNING with a console handler at NOTSET. A child logger set to INFO logs log.info('x'). Is it printed?
options: No, the root's WARNING level blocks it
Yes, propagation checks only handler levels, not parent logger levels
Only if the child has its own handler
quiz.explain: Propagation hands messages straight to parent handlers without checking the parent loggers' levels again.

concepts.name: Logging exceptions
concepts.summary: Record full tracebacks with logger.exception() or exc_info=True, and add the chain of calls with stack_info.
concepts.why: An error log without a traceback is the hardest kind of bug report to act on.
concepts.body:
Inside an `except` block, `log.exception("message")` logs at ERROR and adds the current exception's traceback. It's the same as `log.error("message", exc_info=True)`.

Use `exc_info=True` with other levels when the failure isn't really an error, for example a call you're about to try again: `log.warning("retrying", exc_info=True)`. You can also pass the exception itself: `exc_info=err`.

Guidelines:

- Call `log.exception` only inside an `except` block; elsewhere there is no current exception and you get `NoneType: None` as the "traceback".
- Log **or** re-raise, not both at every layer, or a single failure appears five times. Log where you handle the error (for example, in the top-level code that handles each incoming request).
- Put identifiers in the message: `log.exception("charge failed for order %s", order_id)`.

`stack_info=True` adds the current **call stack** (the chain of function calls that led to this line, without any exception) to a message. That's useful for "who is still calling this old function we want to remove?". `stacklevel=2` credits the message's `funcName` and `lineno` to the caller, which is what you want inside your own logging helper functions.

Exception chains (`raise ... from err`) are printed in full, the same as an uncaught exception.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("billing")

def charge(order_id, amount):
    try:
        return 100 / amount
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        log.exception("charge failed for order %s", order_id)
        return None

charge("A-17", 0)
# ERROR charge failed for order A-17
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "...", line 7, in charge
#     return 100 / amount
# ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
takeaways: log.exception() = log.error() plus the current traceback
exc_info=True attaches a traceback at any level
Log an error once, where it is handled
pitfalls: Logging and re-raising at every layer, so one failure produces many identical tracebacks.

quiz.q: What is the difference between log.exception('x') and log.error('x')?
options: error() can't be used inside except blocks
exception() also records the current traceback

concepts.name: Configuring with dictConfig
concepts.summary: Describe all your loggers, handlers and formatters as one dictionary with logging.config.dictConfig.
concepts.why: One readable settings dict (often loaded from a JSON, YAML or TOML file) replaces scattered setup code and works on every machine.
concepts.body:
`logging.config.dictConfig(config)` builds the whole logging setup from a dictionary, the format web frameworks like Django use. Keys:

- `version`: always `1`.
- `formatters`: named formatters (`format`, `datefmt`, `style`, or `"()"` naming a function that builds a custom one).
- `filters`: named filters.
- `handlers`: each with `class`, `level`, `formatter`, and the arguments for creating the handler, such as `filename` or `stream`.
- `loggers`: per-name `level`, `handlers`, `propagate`.
- `root`: the root logger's settings.
- `disable_existing_loggers`: defaults to **True**, which switches off every logger created before the call. Set it to `False` almost always; otherwise module loggers created at import time go silent.

Values like `"ext://sys.stdout"` refer to Python objects, and `"cfg://..."` refers to other parts of the config. Since 3.12 a `QueueHandler` can be set up fully here, including its listener.

Keep the dict in a module or load it from a file (`json.load`, `tomllib.load`), apply it once at startup, and change only the levels between your laptop and the live system. `logging.getHandlerByName("console")` (3.12+) fetches a configured handler later. The older `fileConfig` (INI format) still works but can do less.
concepts.code:
import logging, logging.config

CONFIG = {
    "version": 1,
    "disable_existing_loggers": False,
    "formatters": {"short": {"format": "%(levelname)s %(name)s: %(message)s"}},
    "handlers": {
        "console": {"class": "logging.StreamHandler", "level": "INFO",
                    "formatter": "short", "stream": "ext://sys.stdout"},
    },
    "loggers": {"urllib3": {"level": "WARNING"}},
    "root": {"level": "DEBUG", "handlers": ["console"]},
}
logging.config.dictConfig(CONFIG)

logging.getLogger("myapp").info("configured")    # INFO myapp: configured
logging.getLogger("urllib3").info("noise")       # filtered by level
print(logging.getHandlerByName("console").level) # 20
takeaways: dictConfig sets up formatters, handlers, loggers and root from one dict
Set disable_existing_loggers to False
ext:// and cfg:// point to Python objects and other config entries
pitfalls: Leaving disable_existing_loggers at its default True, silencing loggers created at import time.

quiz.q: After dictConfig with defaults, loggers created at import time stop logging. Why?
options: dictConfig resets all levels to CRITICAL
Module loggers need their own handlers
quiz.explain: Unless set to False, existing loggers not named in the config are disabled.

concepts.name: Adding context: extra, adapters, filters
concepts.summary: Attach request IDs and other context to log messages with extra=, LoggerAdapter, or a filter reading a context variable.
concepts.why: When a server handles many requests at the same time, their log lines mix together; without a per-request ID they're impossible to untangle.
concepts.body:
Three ways to add fields to log records:

**`extra=`** on a single call: `log.info("paid", extra={"order_id": 42})` adds attributes to the record, usable in formats as `%(order_id)s`. A format that uses a field will fail on records that lack it, and keys must not clash with built-in attributes such as `message` or `asctime`.

**`LoggerAdapter`** wraps a logger and adds the same extra to every call: `LoggerAdapter(log, {"user": "ada"})`. Since 3.13, `merge_extra=True` merges per-call `extra` with the adapter's instead of throwing it away.

**A filter** is any function, or object with a `filter(record)` method, added to a logger or handler. Return False to drop the record, or change it and return True. Returning a (possibly new) `LogRecord` is also allowed since 3.12. Filters on a **handler** see every record reaching it, including ones propagated from other loggers. So a handler filter that reads the current request ID from a **context variable** (a `contextvars.ContextVar`, whose value is kept separately for each thread and each asyncio task) stamps every line, from any module, with no changes where messages are logged. This works even when many requests run at once.

Filters on a logger only run for records created by that exact logger, not its children.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys, contextvars
request_id = contextvars.ContextVar("request_id", default="-")

class RequestIdFilter(logging.Filter):
    def filter(self, record):
        record.request_id = request_id.get()
        return True                          # keep the record

h = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
h.addFilter(RequestIdFilter())
h.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("[%(request_id)s] %(name)s %(message)s"))
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, handlers=[h])

def handle(rid):
    request_id.set(rid)
    logging.getLogger("app.db").info("query")

handle("req-1")                              # [req-1] app.db query
base = logging.LoggerAdapter(logging.getLogger("app"), {"user": "ada"})
base.info("hi %s", base.extra["user"])       # [req-1] app hi ada
takeaways: extra={...} adds fields to one record
LoggerAdapter adds fixed context to every call
A handler filter reading a ContextVar stamps request IDs everywhere
pitfalls: Putting a filter on a parent logger and expecting it to run for child loggers' records.

quiz.q: A filter is attached to logger 'app'. A record from 'app.db' propagates up. Does the filter run?
options: Yes, filters apply to the whole subtree
No, logger filters only see records created by that logger
quiz.explain: Attach to a handler to see propagated records.

concepts.name: Logging in libraries
concepts.summary: Log from reusable packages correctly: named loggers, a NullHandler, and no configuration.
concepts.why: A library that sets up logging itself overrules its users' choices and floods their output.
concepts.body:
Applications set up logging; libraries only **write messages**. Rules for library code:

- Use `logging.getLogger(__name__)` in each module, so users can tune `yourlib` or `yourlib.http` separately.
- Never call `basicConfig`, add handlers to the root, or set levels in code that runs at import time.
- Optionally add `logging.NullHandler()` to your top-level package logger. It does nothing, but it means "this library has a handler", so when the app hasn't set up logging, your warnings don't fall through to `lastResort` on stderr. Python's own docs recommend it for libraries.
- Use DEBUG generously for internal details and WARNING sparingly, only for things the app's owner should act on.
- Don't log and raise the same error; raise it and let the app decide.

From the application side, quiet a chatty library with `logging.getLogger("lib").setLevel(logging.WARNING)`.

`logging.captureWarnings(True)` sends messages from the `warnings` module (for example `DeprecationWarning`s) into the logger named `py.warnings`, so they reach your handlers and log collection service instead of bare stderr.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys, warnings

# --- in yourlib/__init__.py ---
lib_log = logging.getLogger("yourlib")
lib_log.addHandler(logging.NullHandler())

def connect():
    lib_log.debug("opening socket")
    lib_log.warning("using insecure default port")
    warnings.warn("connect() is deprecated", DeprecationWarning)

# --- in the application ---
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, format="%(name)s: %(message)s")
logging.captureWarnings(True)             # warnings -> 'py.warnings' logger
connect()
# yourlib: using insecure default port
# py.warnings: .../app.py:10: DeprecationWarning: connect() is deprecated
#   warnings.warn("connect() is deprecated", DeprecationWarning)
logging.getLogger("yourlib").setLevel(logging.ERROR)  # quiet the library
takeaways: Libraries call getLogger(__name__) and never configure handlers or levels
A NullHandler on the package logger prevents lastResort output
captureWarnings(True) sends warnings into logging
pitfalls: Calling logging.basicConfig at import time in a library, hijacking the application's configuration.

quiz.q: What does adding logging.NullHandler() to a library's top-level logger do?
options: Disables all logging from the library
Sends logs to /dev/null even when the app configures logging
Stops lastResort printing the library's warnings when the app hasn't configured logging
Sets the library's level to CRITICAL
quiz.explain: The handler discards records but its presence stops the fallback; app handlers on ancestors still receive records.

concepts.name: Non-blocking logging with queues
concepts.summary: Move slow handler work (disk and network writes) off your threads with QueueHandler and QueueListener.
concepts.why: Network or disk handlers can stall the threads that handle requests, and the asyncio event loop; a queue separates the two.
concepts.body:
Every handler's `emit()` runs in the thread that logged, and that thread waits until it finishes. A slow destination (email, a web service, a network drive, or even a busy disk) holds up the caller. In asyncio code, that means the event loop.

The fix is logging in two stages:

- `QueueHandler(q)` is the only handler on your loggers. Its `emit` just prepares the record (merges the message, swaps arguments and exception objects that can't be pickled for text) and puts it on a queue. That's fast, and the caller never waits on the slow destination.
- `QueueListener(q, *handlers)` runs a background thread that takes records off the queue and passes them to the real, slow handlers.

Start the listener at startup, and call `listener.stop()` at shutdown to write out the remaining records. Since 3.12, `dictConfig` can create both: a handler with `"class": "logging.handlers.QueueHandler"` and a `"handlers"` list builds a listener, available as `handler.listener`, which you start yourself.

With multiprocessing, a `multiprocessing.Queue` lets worker processes send records to one listener in the main process, which avoids several processes writing into one shared file at once. Record attributes must be picklable then.

Use `respect_handler_level=True` on the listener so each real handler's level still applies.
concepts.code:
import logging, logging.handlers, queue, sys, time

class SlowHandler(logging.StreamHandler):
    def emit(self, record):
        time.sleep(0.2)                    # pretend network I/O
        super().emit(record)

q = queue.Queue(-1)                        # unbounded
listener = logging.handlers.QueueListener(
    q, SlowHandler(sys.stdout), respect_handler_level=True)
log = logging.getLogger("api")
log.addHandler(logging.handlers.QueueHandler(q))
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)

listener.start()
t = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(3):
    log.info("request %d", i)
print(f"logging took {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")  # ~0.000s
listener.stop()                            # flushes: request 0, 1, 2
takeaways: Handlers run in the thread that logged; slow ones hold up the caller
QueueHandler puts records on a queue; QueueListener sends them on from a background thread
Stop the listener at shutdown to write out pending records
pitfalls: Forgetting listener.stop() at exit, losing the last log lines.

quiz.q: Why is QueueHandler recommended for logging from asyncio applications?
options: It keeps slow handler I/O off the event loop thread
It is the only thread-safe handler
quiz.explain: The listener's thread does the I/O; the loop only enqueues.

concepts.name: Structured JSON logs
concepts.summary: Write one JSON object per line with a custom Formatter so log platforms can search every field.
concepts.why: Log search tools used for live systems (ELK, Loki, Datadog, CloudWatch) search by field, not free text.
concepts.body:
On live systems, logs are usually sent to a service that takes them apart again. Plain text needs fragile **regular expressions** (text patterns) to pull values out. **Structured logging** avoids that: each entry is written as JSON Lines, one JSON object per line, with fields such as `time`, `level`, `logger`, `message`, `request_id` and `exc`.

Build it with a `Formatter` subclass whose `format(record)` builds a dict and returns `json.dumps(...)`:

- `record.getMessage()` merges the message and its arguments.
- `record.created` (or `self.formatTime(record)`) gives the time; write it in UTC as ISO 8601 text, like `2026-03-01T12:00:00+00:00`.
- `self.formatException(record.exc_info)` turns a traceback into text when there is one.
- Copy the extra values that came from `extra=` or filters. One approach: compare `record.__dict__` with the attributes of a blank LogRecord.

Keep the message pattern constant and put changing data in fields (`extra={"order_id": 42}`), so the platform can group by message and filter by field.

Third-party packages such as `python-json-logger` and `structlog` do this for you; structlog also lets you attach context once and reuse it. Whatever you choose, use `json.dumps(..., default=str)`, so one value JSON can't handle never breaks the log line.
takeaways: One JSON object per line makes every field searchable
A Formatter subclass builds the dict; use getMessage() and formatException()
Keep messages constant and put changing values in fields
pitfalls: json.dumps without default=str, so one datetime or Decimal in extra breaks the log line.

quiz.q: Why keep the message template constant and pass order IDs via extra?
options: So the platform can group identical events and filter by field
Messages longer than 80 characters are truncated
quiz.explain: Constant messages group together; structured fields stay queryable.

concepts.name: How a log call works inside
concepts.summary: Trace a record from logger call through filters, handlers and locks, and know the performance costs.
concepts.why: Knowing each step lets you explain odd behaviour and keep logging cheap in code that runs very often.
concepts.body:
What `log.info("x %s", v)` does, step by step:

- `isEnabledFor(INFO)` is checked first. The answer is remembered per logger and reset whenever levels change, so calls below the level are very cheap. `logging.disable(level)` stops everything at this point, for all loggers.
- `findCaller()` walks the call stack for file, line and function name, one of the most expensive steps.
- A `LogRecord` is created (through a factory function you can replace with `setLogRecordFactory`), with time, thread, process and the unmerged `msg` and `args`.
- Logger filters run, then `callHandlers` goes through the logger and its parents while `propagate` is True.
- Each handler checks its level, runs its filters, then takes its **lock** (so only one thread uses it at a time) and calls `emit`, which calls `format`. The message is merged with its arguments only now, in `getMessage()`.

Speed tips from the docs: set `logging.logThreads`, `logging.logProcesses`, `logging.logMultiprocessing` and `logging.logAsyncioTasks` (3.12) to False to skip collecting those fields. Avoid building `extra` dicts on every call in loops that run very often. Formatters keep the exception's text in `record.exc_text`, so it's built only once.

Errors inside `emit` go to `handler.handleError`, which prints a traceback but doesn't raise. If `logging.raiseExceptions` is False, they are silently ignored.
concepts.code:
import logging, sys, timeit

log = logging.getLogger("hot")
log.addHandler(logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout))
log.setLevel(logging.WARNING)

n = 100_000
off = timeit.timeit(lambda: log.debug("x=%s", 1), number=n)
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)            # global kill switch
dis = timeit.timeit(lambda: log.warning("x=%s", 1), number=n)
logging.disable(logging.NOTSET)
print(f"filtered debug: {off / n * 1e9:.0f} ns/call")
print(f"disabled:       {dis / n * 1e9:.0f} ns/call")

old = logging.getLogRecordFactory()
def factory(*a, **kw):
    rec = old(*a, **kw); rec.service = "api"; return rec
logging.setLogRecordFactory(factory)
log.handlers[0].setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(service)s %(message)s"))
log.warning("custom field")                  # api custom field
takeaways: Level checks happen first and are remembered, so filtered calls are cheap
findCaller and record creation dominate the cost of emitted calls
Handlers are lock-protected; errors in emit are reported, not raised
pitfalls: Wrapping log calls in try/except: logging already swallows handler errors via handleError.

quiz.q: At what point is the message text actually merged with its arguments?
options: In getMessage(), called while a handler formats the record
quiz.explain: Records carry msg and args separately until a formatter asks for the message.
